title: Understanding prayer (salah)
description: Why Muslims pray, the five daily prayers and their times, how a prayer is put together, and answers to the questions new Muslims ask most about salah.

sections.heading: Why do Muslims pray?
sections.content:
Prayer (salah) is a direct line between you and Allah, with nobody standing in between. Five times a day you stop whatever you are doing to remember your Creator, say thank you, and ask for guidance. It works like an anchor dropped into the middle of an ordinary day.

Prayer feels strange to most new Muslims at first, which is completely normal. Nobody expects you to have it down overnight. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said, **"Pray as you have seen me pray"** (Sahih al-Bukhari 631), and watching and learning takes time. Your effort counts even when your pronunciation is rough or you lose your place.

Prayer also feeds something. Your body needs food and water on a schedule, and your soul needs contact with Allah on one too. Many Muslims describe a settled, clear feeling afterward that they cannot get any other way. Give it a few months and salah often becomes the part of the day you look forward to.

Prayer is an invitation from Allah to come closer to Him. The fact that you are reading about how to do it says something about your sincerity, and sincerity is what Islam asks for most.

sections.heading: The five daily prayers
sections.content:
There are five obligatory prayers each day, spread from dawn to night. Each one has its own time window, and learning those windows is one of the first jobs of a new Muslim:

- **Fajr.** The pre-dawn prayer, performed before sunrise, 2 units (rak'ahs). Getting up for it is hard at first. Many Muslims end up calling it the best prayer of the day.
- **Dhuhr.** The midday prayer, performed after the sun passes its highest point, 4 rak'ahs. It usually lands near a lunch break, which makes it an easy pause in a workday.
- **Asr.** The afternoon prayer, performed mid to late afternoon, 4 rak'ahs.
- **Maghrib.** The sunset prayer, performed just after the sun goes down, 3 rak'ahs.
- **Isha.** The night prayer, performed once twilight is gone, 4 rak'ahs.

Prayer times move with the position of the sun, so they shift through the year. Many Muslims use a prayer time app or website for the exact times where they live. Most mosques post the daily times as well.

You do not have to pray at the exact minute a window opens. Each prayer can be performed anywhere inside its window. That flexibility is deliberate mercy, because life is busy and Islam accounts for it.

sections.heading: The basic structure of a prayer
sections.content:
Every prayer is built from units called **rak'ahs**. Each rak'ah has you standing, bowing, and prostrating. One rak'ah, simplified:

1. **Standing (Qiyam):** You stand facing the Qiblah (the direction of Makkah), raise your hands, and say "Allahu Akbar" (God is the Greatest) to begin. Then you recite Surah Al-Fatiha, the opening chapter of the Quran, followed by a short surah or a few verses.
2. **Bowing (Ruku):** You bow at the waist with your hands on your knees and say "Subhana Rabbiyal Adheem" (Glory to my Lord, the Most Great) three times.
3. **Standing briefly:** You rise from bowing saying "Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah" (Allah hears the one who praises Him), then, standing straight, "Rabbana wa lakal-hamd" (Our Lord, to You belongs all praise).
4. **Prostration (Sujud):** You put your forehead, nose, hands, knees, and toes on the ground and say "Subhana Rabbiyal A'la" (Glory to my Lord, the Most High) three times.
5. **Sitting briefly:** You sit up between the two prostrations and say "Rabbighfir li" (My Lord, forgive me).
6. **Second prostration:** You prostrate again and repeat the same words.

After the second rak'ah you sit and recite the **Tashahhud** (testimony of faith). In the final sitting you also send blessings upon the Prophet (the salawat). You close the prayer by turning your head to the right and then to the left, saying **"Assalamu Alaikum wa Rahmatullah"** (Peace and mercy of Allah be upon you).

Do not try to memorize all of this at once. Start with what you can hold and add to it. Most new Muslims learn Surah Al-Fatiha and the movements first, then fill in the rest over the following weeks.

sections.heading: Preparing for prayer
sections.content:
Before you pray, there are a few things to take care of:

**Wudu (ablution):** Wudu is a short washing ritual that puts you in a state of purity for prayer. You wash your hands, rinse your mouth and nose, wash your face, wash your arms to the elbows, wipe your head, and wash your feet. It stays valid until something breaks it: using the restroom, passing gas, sleeping deeply, and so on.

**A clean place:** Pray somewhere clean. Many Muslims use a prayer mat, and any clean surface will do, including a towel, a carpet, or the floor.

**Appropriate clothing:** Your clothing should be clean and cover the required areas. For men that means at least from the navel to the knees. For women it means the whole body except the face and hands.

**Facing the Qiblah:** Face the direction of the Ka'bah in Makkah. A compass app or a Qiblah finder will give you the direction from wherever you are. If you genuinely cannot work it out, make your best guess. Allah takes the effort and the intention.

**Intention (niyyah):** Set your intention in your heart before you start. Nothing needs to be said out loud, and knowing which prayer you are about to perform is enough. What counts is sincerity, not a formula of words.

sections.heading: Extra prayers you will see, and when to add them
sections.content:
At the masjid you will see people pray extra rak'ahs before and after the obligatory prayer. These are voluntary. They are not part of the obligatory prayer, and nobody owes them.

**The regular sunnah prayers.** The Prophet (peace be upon him) said that whoever prays twelve voluntary rak'ahs in a day and night will have a house built for them in Paradise (Sahih Muslim 728a). A narration in Jami at-Tirmidhi (415, graded Sahih by Darussalam) lists them:

- 2 before Fajr
- 4 before Dhuhr and 2 after it
- 2 after Maghrib
- 2 after Isha

The two before Fajr are among the few that the AMJA answer on travel keeps even on a journey.

**Witr.** An odd-numbered prayer that closes the night. The Prophet said, **"Make witr your last prayer at night"** (Sahih al-Bukhari 998), and taught that night prayer is prayed two rak'ahs at a time, with one rak'ah at the end as witr (Sahih al-Bukhari 990). How firm it is and how it is prayed differ between the schools. The Maliki summary we link counts it as the one confirmed daily sunnah. Ask your teacher how your community prays it.

**Night prayer (tahajjud).** Voluntary prayer in the night, praised in the Quran (17:79). The Prophet's night prayer, in Ramadan and outside it, did not go beyond eleven rak'ahs (Sahih al-Bukhari 1147).

**Forenoon prayer (duha).** Two rak'ahs in the morning, after the sun is up, count as charity for every joint of the body (Sahih Muslim 720).

**Greeting the masjid.** Two rak'ahs when you walk into a masjid, before you sit (Sahih al-Bukhari 444). The schools differ on praying them once the Friday sermon has started, and the salah companion explains how.

**Tarawih in Ramadan.** Voluntary night prayers in Ramadan, often prayed together at the masjid. The Prophet led them on a few nights, then stopped for fear they would be made obligatory (Sahih al-Bukhari 1129). Masjids differ in how many rak'ahs they pray, and you can leave whenever you need to.

**The schools count them differently.** The Maliki summary we link lists two before Fajr, four before and after Dhuhr, four before Asr and two or more after Maghrib, with nothing set after Friday prayer. The Hanafi text we link lists four before Friday prayer and four after it.

**One suggested order, not a rule.** Once the five obligatory prayers feel steady, add one extra at a time. For example, the two before Fajr in your second month, witr before bed in your third, and others later. Taking on witr, night prayer and duha all at once can leave you worn out and tempted to drop everything.

sections.heading: Praying while travelling
sections.content:
Allah allows the prayer to be shortened on a journey (Quran 4:101), and the Prophet (peace be upon him) prayed two rak'ahs instead of four all the way from Madinah to Makkah and back, including a ten-day stay (Sahih al-Bukhari 1081). The details differ between the schools. Choose one school's method with a teacher and keep to it, rather than taking one school's distance and another school's combining rules.

**Shortening (qasr).** Dhuhr, Asr and Isha drop from four rak'ahs to two. Fajr stays at two and Maghrib stays at three. Travel days do not cancel any prayer: you still pray all five.

**Who counts as a traveller.** It depends on the school:

- In the Hanafi answer we link, you are going somewhere at least about 77 km from home and will stay there less than 15 days. Shortening is then required (wajib).
- In the Shafi'i answer, you have passed your city's limits on a trip of more than about 79 to 80 km, and you will not stay four days or more, not counting the days you arrive and leave. Shortening is permitted, with the intention made at the start of the prayer.
- The AMJA (Assembly of Muslim Jurists of America) answer says you may shorten and combine once you have left your town, for as long as you do not intend to settle where you are. It gives no fixed number of days.

We have not yet checked the Maliki and Hanbali distances in their own sources.

**Combining (jam').** The Prophet joined Maghrib and Isha when he was in a hurry on a journey (Sahih al-Bukhari 1106). The schools read this differently:

- In the Shafi'i answer, a traveller can pray Dhuhr with Asr, or Maghrib with Isha, in the time of the first, on three conditions: pray them in order, intend to combine during the first prayer, and pray the second straight after the first.
- In the Hanafi school, truly praying two prayers in one time is valid only at Arafah and Muzdalifah during Hajj. What a Hanafi can do is pray the first prayer just before its time ends and the second just after its time begins. The same Hanafi answer adds that a Hanafi may follow another school's combining rules, as long as every condition of that school is met.
- AMJA allows combining on a journey to remove hardship once you have left your town.

**Sunnah prayers on the road.** The AMJA answer keeps only witr and the two rak'ahs before Fajr while travelling. The Hanafi answer says to keep praying the sunnah prayers unless you are in the rush of travel.

**On a plane.** Pray when the time comes in. The Hanafi answer we link says to stand, bow and prostrate if there is space to do so. If you can only pray seated, moving your head for bowing and prostration, it says to repeat that prayer when you land. Face the qibla as best you can.

**In a car.** Stop at a rest area or a quiet spot and pray beside the car or on a patch of clean ground. Before a long drive, look up the prayer times along the route, and keep a qibla app and a small mat or towel in the car.

**Wiping over socks** lasts three days and nights when you are travelling, instead of one. The washing tool has the details.

sections.heading: Questions new Muslims ask about prayer
sections.content:
**"What if I miss a prayer?"**
Make it up as soon as you remember. The Prophet said that whoever forgets a prayer should pray it when they remember it (Sahih al-Bukhari 597). You will oversleep, get stuck in a meeting, or simply forget. Making it up is straightforward: you perform the prayer you missed. There is no shame in it, and the fact that you care enough to make it up is the point. Prayers from the years before you became Muslim are not owed.

**"I don't know any Arabic yet. Can I still pray?"**
Yes. Keep praying while you learn. Until you know Al-Fatihah, a widely taught option is to say short Arabic phrases of remembrance, such as SubhanAllah and Alhamdulillah, in its place. The Prophet taught these to a man who could not memorise any Quran (Sunan Abi Dawud 832, graded Hasan by al-Albani). The schools differ on the details, including reading from a card, and the salah companion sets out each view. Every line you pick up counts.

**"Can I pray at home or do I have to go to the mosque?"**
Anywhere clean works: home, the office, a park, the mosque. Praying at the mosque is encouraged, the Friday (Jumuah) prayer especially, but the five daily prayers do not require it. Pray where you are when the time arrives.

**"What if I make a mistake during prayer?"**
Mistakes are expected while you are learning. If you catch an error, like forgetting a rak'ah, there is a fix called **Sujud al-Sahw** (prostrations of forgetfulness): two extra prostrations near the end of the prayer (Sahih Muslim 571a). The schools teach slightly different methods. Do not lose sleep over this early on. Build the habit first and learn the basics.

**"I feel self-conscious praying in front of others."**
Very common, and understandable. Many new Muslims pray in private until it stops feeling like a performance, and there is nothing wrong with that. Once prayer becomes second nature, most people find they can do it anywhere without thinking about who is watching. Go at your own pace.
